# Proof

**Claim:** Yes. Two regular unit-speed curves in ℝ³ with the same non-vanishing curvature and torsion are necessarily congruent (they differ by a rigid motion of space).

---

Let $\gamma_1, \gamma_2 : I \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be two regular unit-speed curves, parameterized by arc length $s$, with common curvature $\kappa(s) > 0$ and common torsion $\tau(s)$ (both continuous on the interval $I$). The condition $\kappa > 0$ ensures the Frenet frame is well-defined everywhere.

## Frenet–Serret setup

For each curve, let $\{T_i, N_i, B_i\}$ be the Frenet frame ($i = 1, 2$), where $T_i = \gamma_i'$, $N_i = T_i'/\kappa$, and $B_i = T_i \times N_i$. Both frames satisfy the Frenet–Serret equations with the **same** coefficient functions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_i' &= \phantom{-}\kappa\, N_i, \\
N_i' &= -\kappa\, T_i + \tau\, B_i, \\
B_i' &= \phantom{-}\tau\,(-N_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

Equivalently, writing the frame as the orthogonal matrix $F_i(s) = [T_i(s)\;|\;N_i(s)\;|\;B_i(s)] \in SO(3)$, we have

$$F_i'(s) = F_i(s)\, A(s), \qquad A(s) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -\kappa & 0 \\ \kappa & 0 & -\tau \\ 0 & \tau & 0 \end{pmatrix},$$

a **linear** ODE in $F_i$ with the **same** skew-symmetric coefficient matrix $A(s)$ for both curves.

## Matching initial data via a rigid motion

Fix $s_0 \in I$. Both $\{T_1(s_0), N_1(s_0), B_1(s_0)\}$ and $\{T_2(s_0), N_2(s_0), B_2(s_0)\}$ are positively-oriented orthonormal bases of $\mathbb{R}^3$. Hence there exists a **unique** rotation $R \in SO(3)$ sending one frame to the other:

$$R\,T_1(s_0) = T_2(s_0),\quad R\,N_1(s_0) = N_2(s_0),\quad R\,B_1(s_0) = B_2(s_0).$$

Define the rigid motion $M(x) = R\,x + c$ with translation $c = \gamma_2(s_0) - R\,\gamma_1(s_0)$, and set $\tilde\gamma_1 = M \circ \gamma_1$. Then:

- $\tilde\gamma_1(s_0) = \gamma_2(s_0)$,
- the Frenet frame $\{\tilde T, \tilde N, \tilde B\}$ of $\tilde\gamma_1$ satisfies $\tilde T(s_0) = T_2(s_0)$, $\tilde N(s_0) = N_2(s_0)$, $\tilde B(s_0) = B_2(s_0)$,
- $\tilde\gamma_1$ has the **same** curvature $\kappa$ and torsion $\tau$ as $\gamma_2$ (rigid motions preserve curvature and torsion).

## Uniqueness of the frame ODE

The frame $\tilde F(s) = [\tilde T\;|\;\tilde N\;|\;\tilde B]$ and $F_2(s)$ both solve the **same** linear ODE

$$F'(s) = F(s)\,A(s)$$

with the **same** initial condition $\tilde F(s_0) = F_2(s_0)$. Since $A(s)$ is continuous, the standard existence-and-uniqueness theorem for linear ODEs gives

$$\tilde F(s) = F_2(s) \quad \text{for all } s \in I.$$

In particular $\tilde T(s) = T_2(s)$, i.e. $\tilde\gamma_1'(s) = \gamma_2'(s)$ for all $s$.

## Integrating to congruence

Since $\tilde\gamma_1(s_0) = \gamma_2(s_0)$ and $\tilde\gamma_1'(s) = \gamma_2'(s)$ on all of $I$,

$$\tilde\gamma_1(s) - \gamma_2(s) = \int_{s_0}^{s}\bigl(\tilde\gamma_1'(u) - \gamma_2'(u)\bigr)\,du = 0.$$

Therefore $\tilde\gamma_1(s) = \gamma_2(s)$ for every $s \in I$, which is exactly

$$\gamma_2 = M \circ \gamma_1$$

for the rigid motion $M$. $\blacksquare$

---

**Conclusion:** Two regular unit-speed curves sharing the same non-vanishing curvature and torsion differ by a unique orientation-preserving rigid motion of $\mathbb{R}^3$; in particular they are necessarily congruent. This is the uniqueness half of the **Fundamental Theorem of Space Curves**.

### PROOF COMPLETE
